As if to hide from view.
Except a few gray legs under shiny black umbrellas
Running along the gray shiny sidewalks.

sentences.text: The summer and autumn had been so wet,
That in winter the corn was growing yet:
'Twas a sorrowful sight to see, all around,
The grain lie rotting on the ground.
The tops are each a shining square
Shuttles that steadily press through woolly fabric.

sentences.text: There was a crooked man, and he walked a crooked mile.
He found a crooked sixpence upon a crooked stile.
He bought a crooked cat, which caught a crooked mouse,
And they all lived together in a little crooked house.
Therefore all seasons shall be sweet to thee,
Whether the summer clothe the general earth
With greenness, or the redbreast sit and sing
Betwixt the tufts of snow on the bare branch.

sentences.text: The lonely bridge cuts dark across the marsh
Whose long pools glow with the light
At this end limp bushes overhang,
Palely reflected in the amber-colored water.
I see the tracks of the railroads of the earth;
I see them welding State to State, city to city, through North America;
I see them in Great Britain, I see them in Europe;
I see them in Asia and in Africa.

Shines also upon the checkered rice fields

sentences.text: She stood against the kitchen sink, and looked
Over the sink out through a dusty window
At weeds the water from the sink made tall.
She wore her cape; her hat was in her hand.
High up in the apple tree climbing I go,
With the sky above me, the earth below.
Each branch is the step of a wonderful stair
Which leads to the town I see shining up there.

That in winter the corn was growing yet:
'Twas a sorrowful sight to see, all around,
The grain lie rotting on the ground.
The tops are each a shining square
Shuttles that steadily press through woolly fabric.

sentences.text: There was a crooked man, and he walked a crooked mile.
He found a crooked sixpence upon a crooked stile.
He bought a crooked cat, which caught a crooked mouse,
And they all lived together in a little crooked house.
Therefore all seasons shall be sweet to thee,
Whether the summer clothe the general earth
With greenness, or the redbreast sit and sing
Betwixt the tufts of snow on the bare branch.

sentences.text: She stood against the kitchen sink, and looked
Over the sink out through a dusty window
At weeds the water from the sink made tall.
She wore her cape; her hat was in her hand.
High up in the apple tree climbing I go,
With the sky above me, the earth below.
Each branch is the step of a wonderful stair
Which leads to the town I see shining up there.

passage.text: I hesitated when Rachel invited me to spend a weekend at her family's beach house. I had never liked the ocean. The Pacific water was ice-cold, the salty wind stung my eyes, and I always ended up swallowing too much salt water. But I didn't want to hurt Rachel's feelings, so I eventually agreed to go.

Soon, I found myself wedged into the backseat of Rachel's dad's small car. Rachel chatted excitedly, but when she mentioned swimming in the ocean with me, I shivered and huddled deeper into my sweater. Rachel frowned.
"Annie, did you remember to pack your swimsuit?" Rachel asked.
"No, but I'll be fine in my jeans and T-shirt."
"But the whole point of going to the ocean is to play in the waves together!" Rachel cried.
"I'm not a big fan of playing in the ocean," I finally admitted. "I'll just collect shells instead."
Rachel nodded, a shadow of disappointment falling over her face. She didn't speak for the rest of the ride, and I shifted guiltily in my seat.

When we arrived, Rachel raced to the water while I began to stroll along the shore. My eyes darted over the sand in search of shells. I picked up a beautiful wedge shell, then spotted a clam shell. I loved trying to imagine what cool ocean creatures had made these shells their homes.
Nearby, Rachel let out a shriek and sprang from the water. She ran over to me. "I-I stepped on something slimy!" she stammered.
"Oh, it's probably just seaweed," I told her, and I returned my attention to the shells.
Suddenly, a large wave broke, sending water rushing up the sand. Unable to escape it, I watched it flood over my knees.

Before I could complain about my wet jeans, I noticed something twitch near my soggy sneaker. I kneeled down to get a closer look at the fish that had washed up beside me. It had amber scales and bulging eyes. I called Rachel over to have a look. We watched it squirm in the sand and then get carried back to the ocean with the next wave.

I looked up to see dozens of people in small clusters, observing bunches of the same amber fish. Just then, another wave hit, dropping a new batch of fish onto the shore and carrying other fish back to the ocean. I boldly scooped up one of these beautiful fish and held it in the air while Rachel's mom snapped a picture. I walked into the water and released the fish, watching as it swam away.
My hands were numb with cold, the salt itched my eyes, and my sopping wet clothes rubbed like sandpaper against my skin. But in that moment, I didn't care.

Rachel and I spent the rest of the day leaping through the waves, gathering and releasing fish together. I found myself smiling, and I forgot all about how much I used to hate the ocean. Who knew it had so many slimy, scaly gifts to offer?

passage.text: When he heard the Commercial Street Grill was hiring, Andrew leaped into his car to head downtown. He turned the key, and the car started—this time. Lately the car had been acting up, and fixing it was becoming very costly. Andrew had his eye on a shiny red car that was for sale near his college campus. He desperately wanted the new car, but first he would need to earn some money.
"I'm here to apply for a job," he told the manager of the Grill.
"Great!" she said. "Do you have experience waiting tables?"
"No," Andrew admitted. He had never worked in an actual restaurant before. "But I know I love serving food to people."
He talked about how much fun he'd had helping his aunt at a large party she'd hosted one summer. He'd served refreshments to people sitting at tables in her backyard.
The manager handed Andrew a Commercial Street Grill shirt and told him to come back Friday at four o'clock.
Andrew was trained by another server named Paula. He trailed her around the restaurant to see how she wrote down orders from people. Then he watched as she typed them into the computer.
"Each table is labeled with a number," Paula said. "Make sure you memorize them. And memorize the lunch, dinner, and dessert menus. Know the ingredients of everything."
Andrew didn't see why. Who asks about ingredients? All he noticed was that Paula's customers left large tips for her. If Andrew made that much money, the red car would soon be his.
The following weekend, Andrew was on his own. At the first booth he approached, a customer had a question.
"Is there flour in the baked chicken breast?"
"Um, I don't know," Andrew replied. "Let me ask the chef."
As Andrew walked away, another customer got his attention.
"Excuse me! Does the seafood pasta have shellfish?"
"I'll ask the chef," Andrew responded.
"Can you also ask if there's any butter in the asparagus?" someone else asked.

The questions piled up fast as the tables quickly filled. He couldn't believe how difficult the job became when he didn't know the answers. Andrew had expected to be busy, but this felt like complete chaos. He fell far behind in his tasks, aware of how many people were waiting. They were waiting for answers to questions, and for their drinks, dinners, desserts, and checks.
The stress made Andrew frantic and clumsy. He dropped a whole tray of drinks on the floor.
"I'm sorry," he said to the manager, as he tried to clean up the mess.
"What happened?" she asked.
"Paula told me to memorize everything, but I really didn't prepare," he confessed.
"Ah, so you've learned the hard way," the manager sighed. "Tell you what. Why don't you take a week to study and try again next Friday?"
Andrew considered it. He'd lose a week of tips—but those tips would be small if he didn't improve as a server. Plus the customers would be happier if Andrew knew what he was doing.
"Yes, thanks!" Andrew told the manager. "Next week, I'll be ready for anything!"

passage.text: Slowly but surely, Arin and his grandparents were making progress. Boxes of all sizes were piling up throughout the house. Arin's grandparents had lived in the house for decades and had gathered many possessions. Arin was helping them pack up everything from dusty knickknacks to pieces of furniture. They were going to a smaller house nearby, and Arin was grateful they weren't moving too far away.

The dining room was full of fragile keepsakes, many from India, where his grandparents were born. Arin ripped long pieces of packing paper to wrap his grandparent's dishes. Then he carefully stacked the chinaware in a box. Arin had fond memories of eating from the red, yellow, and blue plates during holidays.

Arin finished taping up the box of dinner plates. He lifted it up to move it out of the way, but the box was very heavy. It slipped from his arms and crashed to the floor. All three of them heard the plates shatter.
"I'm sorry!" Arin apologized.
"It's okay," his grandfather said quietly. "It was an accident."

They opened the box and, sure enough, many of the plates were broken. Only a few of them remained whole. Arin knew the plates were from his grandparents' native country. They had been passed down from another generation. Arin cringed. He felt terrible.
"It was an accident," his grandmother repeated, patting him on the back. "Don't worry."
Carefully, they put the broken pieces into a garbage bag. Arin's grandfather carried the bag to a garbage can in their garage.
They continued packing for a little while, but Arin still felt guilty. He struggled to think of a way to make it up to his grandparents.
Soon Arin saw his father's car pull into their driveway.
"I have to go," he said. "My dad is here to pick me up."
He kissed them both and left through the garage. Arin saw the bag of broken plate pieces and grabbed it.
"What's that?" his father asked, as Arin climbed into the car.
Arin looked at the bag in his hands as an idea came to him. "This," he said, "is an art project."

The following day, he went to the store and purchased everything he needed. At home, Arin went to work. He used a thin board shaped like a rectangle as the base. He took the colorful plate pieces and glued them in a creative arrangement on the board. Arin let the glue dry overnight, and then he filled the spaces with white grout. Finally, he sealed the red, yellow, and blue artwork with a glossy spray. When it was dry, Arin wrapped it up.
A few days later, his family gathered at his grandparents' new house. Arin handed his grandparents his gift and smiled as they unwrapped the artwork.
Arin's grandfather gasped as he figured out where the artwork came from. "This is amazing!"
"I can't wait to hang it in our new home," Arin's grandmother said as she gave him a big hug.

passage.text: Slowly but surely, Arin and his grandparents were making progress. Boxes of all sizes were piling up throughout the house. Arin's grandparents had lived in the house for decades and had gathered many possessions. Arin was helping them pack up everything from dusty knickknacks to pieces of furniture. They were going to a smaller house nearby, and Arin was grateful they weren't moving too far away.

The dining room was full of fragile keepsakes, many from India, where his grandparents were born. Arin ripped long pieces of packing paper to wrap his grandparent's dishes. Then he carefully stacked the chinaware in a box. Arin had fond memories of eating from the red, yellow, and blue plates during holidays.

Arin finished taping up the box of dinner plates. He lifted it up to move it out of the way, but the box was very heavy. It slipped from his arms and crashed to the floor. All three of them heard the plates shatter.
"I'm sorry!" Arin apologized.
"It's okay," his grandfather said quietly. "It was an accident."

They opened the box and, sure enough, many of the plates were broken. Only a few of them remained whole. Arin knew the plates were from his grandparents' native country. They had been passed down from another generation. Arin cringed. He felt terrible.
"It was an accident," his grandmother repeated, patting him on the back. "Don't worry."
Carefully, they put the broken pieces into a garbage bag. Arin's grandfather carried the bag to a garbage can in their garage.
They continued packing for a little while, but Arin still felt guilty. He struggled to think of a way to make it up to his grandparents.
Soon Arin saw his father's car pull into their driveway.
"I have to go," he said. "My dad is here to pick me up."
He kissed them both and left through the garage. Arin saw the bag of broken plate pieces and grabbed it.
"What's that?" his father asked, as Arin climbed into the car.
Arin looked at the bag in his hands as an idea came to him. "This," he said, "is an art project."

The following day, he went to the store and purchased everything he needed. At home, Arin went to work. He used a thin board shaped like a rectangle as the base. He took the colorful plate pieces and glued them in a creative arrangement on the board. Arin let the glue dry overnight, and then he filled the spaces with white grout. Finally, he sealed the red, yellow, and blue artwork with a glossy spray. When it was dry, Arin wrapped it up.
A few days later, his family gathered at his grandparents' new house. Arin handed his grandparents his gift and smiled as they unwrapped the artwork.
Arin's grandfather gasped as he figured out where the artwork came from. "This is amazing!"
"I can't wait to hang it in our new home," Arin's grandmother said as she gave him a big hug.

passage.text: Roberto was staring at the soggy, coffee-stained library book in his hands.
"I'm sorry, ma'am," Roberto told the library customer. "You know the rules. If a book isn't returned in the same condition as it was borrowed in, no taking out new books for two weeks."
"Oh, come on," the customer pleaded. "Aren't rules meant to be broken?"
Roberto said the same thing to her that he said to everyone. "If I break the rules for one person, I have to do it for everyone."
The customer stalked off, huffing with annoyance. Roberto was used to it. As the head librarian of Harbor Hill Library, he was known for his strict rules.

Roberto thought about a memory from his childhood. His brother had received a library book that was sticky with food stains and full of ripped pages. His brother was so disgusted that it was years before he took out another book from the library. That memory taught Roberto that rules were needed to make sure everyone could enjoy the library.
Roberto got up and wandered around the library. In the reference section, he found two teenagers shrieking with laughter while they watched a video.
"Excuse me, but you need to keep your voices down," Roberto reminded them. "You know the rules."
The teenagers rolled their eyes but lowered their voices.
Roberto looked over at a quiet girl sitting at a table nearby. She was clearly trying to study for an exam. If he didn't protect her study space, who would?
Roberto made his way back to the front desk. Soon, he was approached by a boy returning a copy of A Wrinkle in Time.
"I love this book!" exclaimed Roberto. "Did you enjoy it?"
"I couldn't put it down!" said the boy. "Can you help me find the other books in the series?"
"Of course," said Roberto with a smile.
Then he flipped through the book. It was full of writing. "You know you're not supposed to write in library books," Roberto reminded him.
The boy hung his head. "I'm sorry. I was just so excited."
"Unfortunately, the rule is that when books aren't returned in good condition, you're not allowed to take out any new books for two weeks," Roberto explained.
"Oh no!" the boy cried. "So that means I have to wait to read the rest of the series?"
Roberto hesitated. He looked closer at the writing in the library book. The underlining and notes were clearly the work of someone who loved this book and wanted to keep track of his favorite parts.
He remembered his own motto, If I break the rules for one person, I have to do it for everyone. But he also remembered his main goal: to make sure everyone could enjoy what the library had to offer.
"You know what?" Roberto said. "Instead, why don't I have you come volunteer at the library to make up for the book damages? What do you think?"
"Oh, sure, I'd be happy to," the boy said. "I love libraries!"
"That makes two of us," Roberto replied.

passage.text: If anyone ever asked what his favorite school subject was, Randy did not hesitate.
"Science!" he said.

Randy fell in love with science during his first class in the lab, when the students prepared slides with small pieces of onion to examine under microscopes. Randy peered through the lens, and what he saw took his breath away. There, heavily magnified over the bright light, were the cells of the onion. They fit together as snuggly as possible. Each had a cell wall and nucleus. Randy was astounded that a tiny magnificent quilt made up such an ordinary form of life.

The idea that all living things are made up of cells was amazing to Randy. During his other classes, he looked around at the people and plants in the classroom and thought about all the trillions of cells that formed them. That's why Randy loved science class: it introduced him to new ideas. Science changed the way he saw the world around him.
Randy had more trouble connecting with his other classes, like English. One afternoon, his English teacher gave the class a writing assignment.
"Write your own story," Mr. Treadwell said. "Be as creative as you'd like. Just remember to use the elements we've talked about in class."

The bell rang, and Randy's classmates spoke excitedly about writing their own stories. But Randy didn't feel too confident about it. When he climbed onto the school bus, he gazed out the window and thought about how much he'd rather research scientific discoveries than make up his own story.

Days passed, and Randy struggled to think of a plot idea that didn't bore him. With two days left until the story was due, Randy realized he absolutely had to begin writing. He went to the library after school and sat down at a computer, but he just ended up staring at a blank page on the screen.

There was a slim book on the table that was titled Aliens of Planet Zyron. The cover pictured a creature with several eyes and scaly skin, on a planet in another solar system. Randy opened the book and devoured the story about the aliens. The story used scientific terms to describe the structure of their many eyes. Randy loved reading about the ways their eyes detected light and helped them in battle against other alien life-forms.

It was a story that used the elements Mr. Treadwell talked about in English class, like characters, plot, and conflict. But there was plenty of biology in the story, too. What excited Randy was how the author used her imagination to invent a whole new organism.
Randy opened his notebook. He thought about the onion cells again, but this time in a whole new way. What if those cells weren't your ordinary onion cells? What if they had minds of their own?
Randy's fingers began to fly on the keyboard as his story practically wrote itself.

passage.text: If anyone ever asked what his favorite school subject was, Randy did not hesitate.
"Science!" he said.

Randy fell in love with science during his first class in the lab, when the students prepared slides with small pieces of onion to examine under microscopes. Randy peered through the lens, and what he saw took his breath away. There, heavily magnified over the bright light, were the cells of the onion. They fit together as snuggly as possible. Each had a cell wall and nucleus. Randy was astounded that a tiny magnificent quilt made up such an ordinary form of life.

The idea that all living things are made up of cells was amazing to Randy. During his other classes, he looked around at the people and plants in the classroom and thought about all the trillions of cells that formed them. That's why Randy loved science class: it introduced him to new ideas. Science changed the way he saw the world around him.
Randy had more trouble connecting with his other classes, like English. One afternoon, his English teacher gave the class a writing assignment.
"Write your own story," Mr. Treadwell said. "Be as creative as you'd like. Just remember to use the elements we've talked about in class."

The bell rang, and Randy's classmates spoke excitedly about writing their own stories. But Randy didn't feel too confident about it. When he climbed onto the school bus, he gazed out the window and thought about how much he'd rather research scientific discoveries than make up his own story.

Days passed, and Randy struggled to think of a plot idea that didn't bore him. With two days left until the story was due, Randy realized he absolutely had to begin writing. He went to the library after school and sat down at a computer, but he just ended up staring at a blank page on the screen.

There was a slim book on the table that was titled Aliens of Planet Zyron. The cover pictured a creature with several eyes and scaly skin, on a planet in another solar system. Randy opened the book and devoured the story about the aliens. The story used scientific terms to describe the structure of their many eyes. Randy loved reading about the ways their eyes detected light and helped them in battle against other alien life-forms.

It was a story that used the elements Mr. Treadwell talked about in English class, like characters, plot, and conflict. But there was plenty of biology in the story, too. What excited Randy was how the author used her imagination to invent a whole new organism.
Randy opened his notebook. He thought about the onion cells again, but this time in a whole new way. What if those cells weren't your ordinary onion cells? What if they had minds of their own?
Randy's fingers began to fly on the keyboard as his story practically wrote itself.

passage.text: "I can't believe we're finally going!" squeals Roxy. She hops on her hoverboard and powers it on while I open the garage door. Derek turns on his hoverboard, too. They both float a foot or so above the ground, their boards humming. We, along with everyone we know, have been waiting for this day for weeks: the start of GameCon 2059. It's a chance to play all the newest video games before you can buy them. Plus, there are always amazing prizes. Derek's cousin won a whole virtual-reality game system last year!
Derek and Roxy zoom out of the garage and toward the street. I tap the "On" button on my board with my foot, over and over. Nothing.
"Eli, come on!" says Roxy.

"Something's wrong with my board," I say with a sigh, stepping off to take a closer look. Derek and Roxy zoom back over and hop off their boards. Roxy flips mine over and examines it. Meanwhile, I look out at my street, where groups of hoverists go zooming by. I recognize some of them from school.
"I think your motor's just broken," she finally declares. "I don't know if the hover shop can take it on a Saturday."
I feel a pit growing in my stomach. "You guys should just go on without me. You don't want to be late." I picture them exploring a virtual world together, without me.

"No, there has to be a way we can get you there," says Derek, frowning at my board. He takes it from Roxy and shakes it, holding it up to the garage light. Meanwhile, Roxy leans against the wall and stares into space, her eyebrows pulled close together. Finally, she says, "That's it!"
She sprints next door to her house and disappears inside for several minutes. When Roxy returns, she is out of breath and holding some kind of wooden hoverboard with wheels.
"Have you ever seen one of these?" she pants, pointing to the bright red plank.
I shake my head and reach out to take the board.

"This is a skateboard," she explains, handing it to me. "Kids used to ride them before there were hoverboards. This one belonged to my grandma when she was a teenager. Be careful, Eli. I think it's from the 2010s."

Just a few minutes later, we are zooming—and rolling—on our way. Derek and Roxy have slowed down a little bit on their hoverboards so I can keep up. I feel pretty silly wheeling down the road, and I'm getting stares from passing hoverists. But Derek and Roxy insist that it's cool, in an old-fashioned, retro sort of way. Anyway, it doesn't really bother me too much—I know that thanks to my skateboard, I'll soon be at GameCon 2059.

passage.text: "I can't believe we're finally going!" squeals Roxy. She hops on her hoverboard and powers it on while I open the garage door. Derek turns on his hoverboard, too. They both float a foot or so above the ground, their boards humming. We, along with everyone we know, have been waiting for this day for weeks: the start of GameCon 2059. It's a chance to play all the newest video games before you can buy them. Plus, there are always amazing prizes. Derek's cousin won a whole virtual-reality game system last year!
Derek and Roxy zoom out of the garage and toward the street. I tap the "On" button on my board with my foot, over and over. Nothing.
"Eli, come on!" says Roxy.

"Something's wrong with my board," I say with a sigh, stepping off to take a closer look. Derek and Roxy zoom back over and hop off their boards. Roxy flips mine over and examines it. Meanwhile, I look out at my street, where groups of hoverists go zooming by. I recognize some of them from school.
"I think your motor's just broken," she finally declares. "I don't know if the hover shop can take it on a Saturday."
I feel a pit growing in my stomach. "You guys should just go on without me. You don't want to be late." I picture them exploring a virtual world together, without me.

"No, there has to be a way we can get you there," says Derek, frowning at my board. He takes it from Roxy and shakes it, holding it up to the garage light. Meanwhile, Roxy leans against the wall and stares into space, her eyebrows pulled close together. Finally, she says, "That's it!"
She sprints next door to her house and disappears inside for several minutes. When Roxy returns, she is out of breath and holding some kind of wooden hoverboard with wheels.
"Have you ever seen one of these?" she pants, pointing to the bright red plank.
I shake my head and reach out to take the board.

"This is a skateboard," she explains, handing it to me. "Kids used to ride them before there were hoverboards. This one belonged to my grandma when she was a teenager. Be careful, Eli. I think it's from the 2010s."

Just a few minutes later, we are zooming—and rolling—on our way. Derek and Roxy have slowed down a little bit on their hoverboards so I can keep up. I feel pretty silly wheeling down the road, and I'm getting stares from passing hoverists. But Derek and Roxy insist that it's cool, in an old-fashioned, retro sort of way. Anyway, it doesn't really bother me too much—I know that thanks to my skateboard, I'll soon be at GameCon 2059.

passage.text: When Mr. and Mrs. Biggleswade had to travel, they asked the Greeley family next door to look after their vegetable garden while they were away. The Greeleys were happy to help. Even the two Greeley sons, Alex and Anthony, enjoyed weeding and watering the spinach and kale plants.
When the Biggleswades returned home, Mrs. Biggleswade stopped over at the Greeley house, cradling large bunches of leafy vegetables.
"Your family was such a help!" she said. "Our spinach and kale plants look bigger than ever!"
"Oh, that's great to hear," Mrs. Greeley said.
"I wanted to give you some of our spinach and kale to say thank you," Mrs. Biggleswade said, passing the vegetables to Mrs. Greeley.
"Why, thank you!" said Mrs. Greeley, forcing a smile. None of the Greeleys knew much about spinach and kale. She couldn't imagine what they would do with a bunch of leafy greens.
"No problem!" Mrs. Biggleswade said. "I'll swing by later to find out what delicious dishes you cook with them!"
In the Greeley kitchen, the clusters of vegetables appeared even more gigantic. Mrs. Greeley, Mr. Greeley, Anthony, and Alex looked at the deep green vegetables.
"So we have to eat all of that spinach and kale?" Anthony asked, raising his eyebrows.
"I think so," Mrs. Greeley said glumly. "Mrs. Biggleswade said she's going to ask us how we cooked them."
"But none of us like vegetables like these," Alex pointed out.

Mr. and Mrs. Greeley tried to find ways to use the vegetables. Mr. Greeley boiled the spinach and served it as a side dish on pizza night. No one liked eating the soggy, bland greens. The next day, Mrs. Greeley put kale on Alex's bologna sandwich. Alex took a small bite and swallowed hard. The rest of the sandwich sat on his plate.

Mr. and Mrs. Greeley decided they were going to have to get creative. They started to look up interesting recipes that used spinach and kale in tasty ways. That night, Mr. Greeley prepared turkey burgers with chopped spinach inside them. He used garlic and different spices and topped them with some Greek cheese. The Greeleys ate every last bite.
"Best burger ever!" Alex proclaimed.

Still, there was much more kale and spinach left. The following day, Mr. and Mrs. Greeley went to work on another meal—lasagna. This time, they layered the lasagna with fresh kale and mushrooms instead of the usual Italian sausage. The delicious aroma filled the kitchen as the lasagna baked in the oven.
The kale lasagna was so good that Mr. and Mrs. Greeley brought some next door for the Biggleswades to try.
"What a wonderful idea!" Mrs. Biggleswade said. "We never know what to do with all this spinach and kale. We were hoping your family would give us some ideas!"
And that's how the Friday night dinner tradition began—the Biggleswades provided the greens, and the Greeleys figured out what to do with them.

header.text: An adjective is a word that tells about a noun. Adjectives often tell what kind or how many.

sentences.text: The adjective tells what kind of apples they were.

header.text: An adverb is a word that tells about a verb, an adjective, or another adverb. Adverbs often tell how, when, or where.

sentences.text: The adverb really tells how quickly Grace ran.

contents.text: Most adverbs that tell how end in -ly, like the adverb quickly.

header.text: You can't always use -ly to tell whether a word is an adjective or an adverb, though.

sentences.text: Soon is an adverb that doesn't end in -ly.
Friendly is an adjective that ends in -ly.

pro + long → prolong
